newsitem.title: JAPAN: Euro concerns to continue pressuring mark--dealers.
newsitem.headline: Euro concerns to continue pressuring mark--dealers.

text.p: The German mark is likely to weaken further, hammered by expectations that European economic and monetary union (EMU) will start on time, but with a weak single currency, traders and analysts in Tokyo say.
"I think the dollar will keep rising (against the mark)...as naturally as a train stopping at one station after another," said Nobuo Kihara, forex marketing chief at Banque Paribas's Tokyo branch.

The mark resumed its prolonged slide after Monday's release of an independent audit estimating France's 1997 deficit at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), exceeding an earlier official estimate of a more fiscally sound 3.0 percent.

Original criteria for EMU stipulated that the ratio of each nation's deficit to GDP not exceed 3.0 percent, in order to ensure that the European currency would remain strong against the dollar, the yen and other leading world currencies.

On Tuesday, however, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said that Europe's single currency, the euro, could be stable even if France and Germany had deficit-to-GDP ratios of 3.2 or 3.3 percent, apparently conceding that the strict fiscal criteria would not be met.

"I see a change in the Bundesbank's attitude. They used to talk about a strong mark and euro, but they now say the euro will be stable even if EMU begins under looser criteria," said Ryosuke Tsuji, senior vice president and manager of the spot forex department at Societe Generale in Tokyo.

He added that, with no official comments on Tuesday to try to talk up the tumbling mark, concerns eased about possible German central bank buying of marks at current levels. This paved the way for a further dollar advance.
"If the dollar breaks above 1.84 marks and its ascent accelerates, then the market will become more wary of possible intervention," Tsuji said.

In late Tokyo trade on Wednesday, the dollar lurched above 1.83 marks to its highest level against the German currency in nearly six years. At the same time, the mark slid to a two-year low against the yen.
Dealers said speculation that the EMU's launch might be delayed, in order to buy time to shore up government finances and ensure a strong start for the euro, had now widely receded.
"Politically, EMU has to start on time," said Toru Okuni, senior dealer at Dresdner Bank in Tokyo.
He said politicians in Germany will try their hardest to launch the single currency on schedule on January 1, 1999, even if they have to accept a weak euro or mark.
"They (politicians) face elections, so they need to be nice to German exporters, such as automakers, who are not in favour of a strong mark," he added.

Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo, said: "The most important thing to realise is that...in 17 months the Bundesbank will no longer be an independent entity."
He said the possible loss of Bundesbank support for a strong mark would be another factor to weaken the currency in the future.
Chart experts said the next technical target for dollar/mark would be around 1.8420 marks, the previous dollar high hit in July 1991.
Landon said that, if the dollar clearly breaks above that level, it will head towards 2.0 marks, but he doubts that this will occur by the end of this year.
"It will be just too fast... I think traders will start looking at a consolidation phase," Landon said.
